metadata.title: Woman attacked by otter while swimming, gets 38 stitches

sources.news_title: Officials say river otters are rare attackers and are urging visitors to keep away after a swimmer needed rabies shots and 38 stitches.

sources.text:
INCLINE VILLAGE, Nev. — A typical day of swimming turned dangerous for a Nevada woman when she was attacked by an aggressive otter in Lake Tahoe.
Lynnette Bellin, of Reno, was attacked on Sunday while she took a dip in the lake near Hidden Beach on the Nevada side of the Lake, KCRA reported. The ambush by the otter resulted in 38 stitches and rabies shots when she went to an area hospital, according to the television station.
“At first I thought it was a person pulling on me because it was so strong,” Bellin told the Reno Gazette Journal. “I haven’t seen anyone else out there swimming, so I wasn’t sure.
“And then I felt the teeth and claws, and it was relentless.”
Bellin, a swimming instructor, said the harder she fought the otter, the more aggressive the animal became. She told the newspaper that she picked up the otter and tried to throw it.
The otter then began to bite and claw her hands and face, the Gazette reported.
“My only thought was like, I got to get away from this. But it kept following me,” Bellin told KCRA. “I tried to swim away from it at one point and it was just attacking my feet.”
A Reno woman was attacked by an otter while swimming near Hidden Beach on the Nevada side of Lake Tahoe. Full coverage: https://t.co/juVxFqNVi0 pic.twitter.com/JseKinmhUw
— kcranews (@kcranews) September 1, 2026
Ironically, the name of Bellin’s swimming team when she was a child was the Otters, the Gazette reported. She is an avid open-water swimmer and recently returned from a vacation in Laguna Beach, California, where she swam with dolphins and even saw a baby shark.
The other eventually left Bellin alone, but she was worse for wear as she clambered up rocks at the shore.
“When I got out, like 10 feet up the rock, he was just circling the water,” she told KCRA. “I could just hear him breathing heavy and that’s when I was like, there’s no way I’m getting back in there, you know?”
Bellin owns ISR Reno Tahoe, a swim safety and rescue school for adults. She also teaches infant swim rescue classes in Reno and Incline Village, the Gazette reported.
“I even have a little toy otter I use in swim lessons with kids,” she told the newspaper. “I might not use that anymore.”

River Otters: Larger than thought, feistier than expected, and definitely in Lake Tahoe
When you think of a badger or a wolverine, you probably picture a fierce, powerful predator and you’d be right. These tough mammals are part of the family Mustelidae, the weasels, and can occasionally be found in Tahoe alongside several other members of the weasel family. The longest of them all, with some adults reaching four feet in length, is the River Otter, which has certainly been making headlines lately.
The Tahoe region is home, at least occasionally, to seven species of mustelids, including not only the aforementioned North American River Otter, American Badger, and Wolverine but also their cousins, the Long-tailed Weasel, American Short-tailed Weasel, American Mink, and Pacific Marten. Some of these animals can look quite similar, while others appear very different from one another, but they all share characteristics typical of the family: elongated bodies, relatively short legs, small rounded ears, short skulls, and dense fur. Depending on the species, mustelids can be terrestrial, arboreal, or aquatic, with river otters and mink particularly well adapted to life in and around water.
Will Richardson, Executive Director at the Tahoe Institute for Natural Science (TINS), is not surprised that so few Tahoe residents know that we have otters here: “We have been closely tracking the dramatic return of river otters to the area over the last 15 or so years, both through staff observations along the Truckee River and around Donner and Lake Tahoe, as well as through photographs and reports shared with us by members of the community.”
“They are not new invaders to Tahoe, but they were largely absent from the region for many decades, having been trapped out from most of the watershed,” Richardson said. “And for a lot of folks, it can be a little tricky telling them apart from a Mink. Nevertheless, they are a natural part of the region’s wildlife community and are well adapted to living in and around our cold, high-elevation waterways, and seem to be thriving as they repopulate the area.”
In summary, river otters inhabit Tahoe and belong here.
The Otter Incident: Rare but Real
Recently, a swimmer in Lake Tahoe was bitten and injured by a North American River Otter during an open-water swim. The encounter was certainly surprising and understandably generated a lot of attention.
As someone who teaches people about Tahoe’s wildlife, I was surprised by the encounter, but I was also not surprised that an otter, related to other fierce weasels could behave this way. River otters are extremely effective predators, and their bodies are built for hunting in the water, with webbed feet, powerful tails, dense waterproof fur, and strong jaws. Their playful and curious behavior can make them fun to watch, but it is important to always remember that they are wild animals.
We also should not assume we know exactly why this particular otter attacked the swimmer. Without knowing the circumstances from the animal’s perspective, it would be difficult to speculate about its motivation. What we do know is that wild animals can react defensively when they feel threatened, surprised, cornered, or otherwise disturbed, especially with a pup nearby. The best way to avoid a negative wildlife encounter is to give animals plenty of space and allow them a way to move away from us.
Is this attack common? Short answer, no. Did it happen? Yes. Could it happen again? Potentially. It is not unprecedented in the region. In 2023, river otters attacked multiple people in Serene Lakes, near Donner Summit.
I think the bigger lesson is not that people should be afraid of swimming in Lake Tahoe but be aware that we live in a place where people and wildlife share the same landscape. When we hike, swim, paddle, camp, ski, or explore around Lake Tahoe, we are recreating in wildlife habitat. We cannot control what wild animals do and occasionally we may encounter them in unexpected places. That is part of living in a wild landscape alongside other predators that call Tahoe home, including bears, mountain lions, and, increasingly heading our way, wolves.
Does that mean the swimmer should have known this could happen? Absolutely not.
This was an unlucky and unusual encounter, and there is no reason to suggest that she should have expected it, especially in an open-water swimming context, and we feel terrible that it happened. But it does give all of us a good reminder about how to interact with wildlife. Watch them. Photograph them. Learn about them. Enjoy seeing them but most importantly, give them space.
Cute but NOT Cuddly
It is unfortunate that an unusual encounter can overshadow all of the amazing things we know about these animals. River otters are fascinating members of Tahoe’s ecosystem.
They are excellent swimmers and can remain underwater for several minutes at a time. Their dense fur helps insulate them in cold water, and they are active year-round. They can even use snow and ice to their advantage, moving across frozen surfaces by sliding on their bellies and bounding.
Their diet is largely aquatic, with fish and crayfish among their favorite foods. Will Richardson recently shared with me how their intelligence and adaptability has led them to take advantage of novel prey at Point Reyes National Seashore, where they have learned how to drown Brown Pelicans as they swim in the estuaries.
As predators, they play an important role in the streams, rivers, and lakes wherever they live. They are capable of traveling on land by walking, running, or sliding and can move between
tributaries and watersheds in search of food and suitable habitat. And if you have ever seen river otters playing, swimming, feeding, grooming, or sunning themselves along the water, you know just how fun they can be to watch.
Wild animals deserve the opportunity to remain wild, and the best wildlife encounter is one where both you and the animal get to walk, swim, or slide away safely.

A Lake Tahoe swimmer was attacked by a river otter Sunday, leaving her with multiple cuts and wounds that required 38 stitches.
Lynnette Bellin of Reno, Nev., told The Sacramento Bee in a statement that she was taking a morning swim near Hidden Beach on the east side of Lake Tahoe when an otter grabbed her leg.
“I suddenly felt hands on my leg and was pulled underwater. It felt like a human was grabbing me, it was so strong. I turned around and that’s when I saw the otter, and it immediately started attacking me,” Bellin, a certified Infant Swimming Resource Self-Rescue instructor, said in a statement.
The river otter scratched Bellin’s legs as she tried to push it away in an attack she called “long and relentless.” The otter also scratched her face and injured her hands. After several attempts to escape, she was eventually able to get herself on a rock and climb onto some boulders away from it.
Bellin later climbed a fence to get to a bike path, walking three quarters of a mile to her car covered in blood. As she was walking, a passerby saw her and called the authorities. They met her at Hidden Beach and took her to a local emergency department for treatment, where she received 38 stitches and was given a series of rabies shots.
Nevada Department of Fish and Wildlife Spokesperson Kenzie Margiott told The Bee that authorities attempted to trap the river otter in Hidden Beach on Sunday afternoon but were unable to find it. The department is also working with Nevada State Parks on posting warning signs near Hidden Beach.
North American river otters can grow 3 to 4 feet long, including their tail, and weigh between 11 and 30 pounds, according to the National Wildlife Federation. They are native predators in the Tahoe Basin.
Margiott said otters can become violent if they feel threatened or stressed, but noted that otter attacks on humans are uncommon.
The Aug. 30 attack is the second widely reported incident of a river otter assaulting a swimmer in Lake Tahoe in recent weeks. Bob Daly of Stateline, Nev., told South Tahoe Now that he was attacked by an otter on Aug. 9. Daly said he was swimming from his boat to a designated swimming area on Pope Beach when an otter began chasing him. It attacked his legs for four to five minutes while he screamed for help and attempted to swim away.
“It was a cute little Disney moment,” Daly told South Tahoe Now. “Aw, ain’t that cute. It wasn’t cute for very long.”
Daly had eight bite and scratch marks and was also started on rabies treatment.
As for Bellin, she hopes her experience will show people the importance of swimming as a critical life skill.
“I encourage people to prioritize water competency in both adults and giving children the opportunity to learn self-rescue at a young age so that swimming becomes second nature. Because I was a strong swimmer, I was able to concentrate on evading the otter attack and did not respirate water or go under from panic,” Bellin said.
She’ll have to stay out of water while her wounds heal, but she plans on swimming in the lake again when she’s on her feet.
“I look forward to getting back in the water with my swim students and will return to swimming in Lake Tahoe, because it truly is my favorite place in the world to swim,” Bellin said. “I will just choose a different route to swim and will stay far away from where I encountered the otter!”
